reading.body:
Amazon Web Services recorded $717 billion in revenue in 2025 while operating two major AI product lines: SageMaker for full-stack ML lifecycle management and Bedrock for managed foundation model access.

AWS sits at the intersection of compute supply and AI demand. SageMaker's architecture—unified data lakes, model monitoring, bias detection, and governance tools—reflects the infrastructure required to run production AI at scale. Bedrock's API model with VPC support and IAM integration suggests AWS is positioning itself as the managed layer between foundation models and enterprise users who want isolation and control. Both products point to a company treating AI not as a feature but as a platform business spanning data, compute, and model serving.

The scale here matters for power and buildings. A $717 billion revenue company in cloud services operates data centers globally to deliver these products. The fact that SageMaker includes toxicity detection, guardrails, and data lineage tracking indicates AWS is building compliance and observability into the compute layer itself. This is not decorative. As regulatory exposure grows, the infrastructure provider that bakes governance into the platform gains advantage over those that bolt it on later.

The data does not specify AWS's capital spending, energy consumption, or data center locations. It does not break out AI revenue from total AWS revenue or show whether SageMaker and Bedrock are growing faster than legacy services. It does not name which foundation models Bedrock serves or how much compute AWS allocates to these two products versus others.

profile_text.body:
Amazon Web Services presents its site around the next generation of Amazon SageMaker, which it describes as the center for all your data, analytics, and AI. The company says the service brings together AWS machine learning and analytics capabilities in a single development environment, SageMaker Unified Studio, with access to data in data lakes, data warehouses, and third-party or federated sources. It lists model development tools including SageMaker AI with HyperPod, JumpStart, and MLOps, and it describes Amazon Q Developer as the most capable generative AI assistant for software development. The site also covers a lakehouse architecture spanning Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and Amazon Redshift with Apache Iceberg-compatible tools, zero-ETL integrations, governance through Amazon SageMaker Catalog, and open source analytics on Amazon Athena, Amazon EMR, and AWS Glue. Customer statements on the page come from an unnamed automotive operation and from Carrier, both describing use of SageMaker for data unification and governance.

Two products are tracked for the company. Amazon SageMaker is listed for full ML lifecycle management, model monitoring, bias detection, and explainability tools. AWS Bedrock is listed as a managed foundation model API service with IAM integration, VPC support, model evaluation tools, and AgentCore for agent orchestration.

The company profile records Amazon Web Services as a public company, ticker AMZN, CIK 0001018724, founded in 1994 and headquartered in Seattle, WA, USA. Its most recent revenue figure is $716,924,000,000 for the period ending 2025-12-31, reported on Form 10-K. The litigation record includes a case, Haugland v. Anthropic PBC, in the District Court, D. Delaware, and a law exposure entry for Washington with a count of 111.
